title: Signature Quiet-Home Charter
body:
The Signature Quiet-Home Charter is an original Signature design for a household agreement that states, in plain words, what the home senses, what it never senses, and how any member can pause it. The Charter is printed and kept where everyone can see it, and it is written before devices are bought, not after, so that purchases serve the agreement instead of rewriting it. It is a design for governance, not a product, and it is labeled Signature throughout, with speculative elements marked as design rather than established fact.

How to do it: State what the home senses and what it never senses; Give every member a pause right; Write the Charter before buying devices; Print it where everyone can see it; Review it when the household changes.

What to check: Test the Charter by asking each household member to name one sensed thing and one never-sensed thing, and confirm all can answer.

When to stop or get help: Do not let any device operate outside the Charter. A device that breaks the agreement breaks the trust the Charter exists to build.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.
